title: Represent analyse and calculate shape and motion in 2-and 3-dimensional space in different contexts

lessons.title: Two-dimensional shapes: perimeter and area on the farm
lessons.html:
Measuring land and surfaces

Fencing a camp, ordering fertiliser for a land, laying a concrete floor in a packshed or planning a new orchard block all need calculations of perimeter and area.

Units

  • Length: millimetre (mm), centimetre (cm), metre (m), kilometre (km). 1 km = 1 000 m.
  • Area: square metre (m²) and hectare (ha). 1 ha = 10 000 m² (a square of 100 m by 100 m).

Formulas

ShapePerimeterArea
Rectangle2 × (length + breadth)length × breadth
Trianglesum of the three sides½ × base × perpendicular height
Circle2 × π × radiusπ × radius × radius

Use π = 3.14 or the π key on your calculator.

Worked examples

  1. Rectangular camp 400 m by 250 m. Perimeter = 2 × (400 + 250) = 1 300 m of fence line. If you use five strands of wire, you need 5 × 1 300 = 6 500 m of wire, plus extra for joins and gates. Area = 400 × 250 = 100 000 m² = 10 ha.
  2. Triangular corner of a land with base 200 m and perpendicular height 150 m. Area = ½ × 200 × 150 = 15 000 m² = 1.5 ha.
  3. Centre pivot with a radius of 300 m. Irrigated area = 3.14 × 300 × 300 = 282 600 m², about 28.3 ha. The outer wheel travels 2 × 3.14 × 300 = 1 884 m per full circle.

Irregular areas

Divide an irregular land into rectangles and triangles, calculate each and add them together. Today many farms also use GPS or mapping apps, which calculate area from points walked or driven around the boundary; still do a rough check by hand to catch errors.

Pythagoras and square corners

In a right-angled triangle, the longest side squared equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. Builders and fencers use the 3-4-5 method: measure 3 m along one line and 4 m along the other; if the diagonal between those points is exactly 5 m, the corner is square. For a 30 m by 40 m shed floor, the diagonal should be 50 m.

Using area results

Once you know the area, you can work out inputs: at 250 kg of fertiliser per hectare, the 10 ha camp needs 2 500 kg, which is 50 bags of 50 kg.

lessons.title: Three-dimensional objects: volume and capacity
lessons.html:
Tanks, dams, silos and trucks

Volume tells you how much space an object fills or holds. On a farm it is used for water tanks, reservoirs, feed bunkers, grain bins, concrete and loads on a truck.

Units

  • Volume: cubic metre (m³) and cubic centimetre (cm³).
  • Capacity: litre (L) and kilolitre (kL). 1 m³ = 1 000 L = 1 kL.

Formulas

SolidVolume
Rectangular prism (box)length × breadth × height
Cylinderπ × radius × radius × height
Triangular prismarea of triangle end × length
Cone⅓ × π × radius × radius × height

Worked examples

  1. Concrete reservoir 20 m long, 10 m wide, 2 m deep: 20 × 10 × 2 = 400 m³ = 400 000 L.
  2. Round water tank with a diameter of 3 m (radius 1.5 m) and height 2 m: 3.14 × 1.5 × 1.5 × 2 = about 14.1 m³, or roughly 14 100 L. If troughs use 3 500 L a day, a full tank lasts about four days.
  3. Concrete slab for a dairy floor, 12 m by 8 m, 0.1 m (100 mm) thick: 12 × 8 × 0.1 = 9.6 m³. Order a little extra for waste.
  4. Bunker silo with a triangular-shaped heap end of base 6 m and height 2 m, 30 m long: (½ × 6 × 2) × 30 = 180 m³.

Surface area

Surface area is the total area of all the faces of a solid. It is needed for painting a tank, insulating a cold room or wrapping a pallet. A closed box has six rectangular faces; add their areas. The curved side of a cylinder has area 2 × π × radius × height.

Representing 3-D objects

Objects are shown on paper as plans (view from above), elevations (front and side views) and nets (the flat shape that folds into the solid). Being able to read a builder's plan of a new packshed or a cold room helps you check quantities and spot errors before construction.

Units and safety

Always convert all lengths to the same unit before multiplying. A common mistake is mixing 100 mm with metres. Remember also that water is heavy: 1 m³ of water has a mass of about 1 000 kg, so tank stands must be built strong enough.

lessons.title: Scale, position and motion
lessons.html:
Maps, plans and moving objects

Scale

A scale shows how a drawing relates to real size. On a map with a scale of 1:50 000, 1 cm on the map represents 50 000 cm = 500 m on the ground. So 4 cm on the map = 200 000 cm = 2 km. On a farm plan drawn at 1:100, a shed 15 cm long on paper is 15 m long in reality.

Position and direction

Positions can be given by grid references on a map, or by GPS coordinates (latitude and longitude) used in mapping apps, precision farming and to send a location to emergency services. Directions are given by compass points or bearings measured clockwise from north. Knowing how to give a clear location (farm name, nearest road, landmark and GPS pin) can save lives in an emergency.

Transformations

Shapes can be moved without changing size: translated (slid), reflected (mirrored) or rotated (turned). Enlargement changes size by a scale factor. Planting patterns in orchards and the layout of shade-net structures use these ideas: the same block is repeated across a land.

Speed, distance and time

Speed = distance ÷ time, so distance = speed × time and time = distance ÷ speed.

  • A bakkie travels 90 km to the co-op at 60 km/h: time = 90 ÷ 60 = 1.5 hours.
  • A tractor sprays with a 12 m boom at 8 km/h. In one hour it travels 8 000 m and covers 8 000 × 12 = 96 000 m² = 9.6 ha in theory. Turning, filling and overlaps reduce the real work rate.

Rates

Rates compare two quantities with different units: litres per hectare, kilograms per animal per day, revolutions per minute. Example: a pump delivering 5 L per second fills a 14 100 L tank in 14 100 ÷ 5 = 2 820 seconds, which is 47 minutes.

Graphs of motion

A distance-time graph shows how far something has moved. A straight sloping line means constant speed; a flat line means it is standing still; a steeper line means faster movement. Truck trackers and logbooks produce such graphs for fleet managers.

Key points

  • 1 ha = 10 000 m² and 1 m³ = 1 000 L.
  • Rectangle area = length × breadth; triangle = ½ × base × height; circle = π × r × r.
  • Box volume = l × b × h; cylinder volume = π × r × r × h.
  • Convert all measurements to the same unit before calculating.
  • Speed = distance ÷ time; map scale 1:50 000 means 1 cm = 500 m.
